newsitem.title: UK: Emerging market bonds moving into the mainstream.
newsitem.headline: Emerging market bonds moving into the mainstream.

text.p: A larger and more diverse group of investors, especially from the U.S., now buys emerging market bonds than ever before and this trend is set to continue, bankers said on Thursday.

This so-called cross-over buying -- when non-emerging market specialists buy emerging market debt -- has buoyed Latin American bond spreads and explained the huge success of recent jumbo dollar bonds.
"There is definitely a trend towards more cross-over buying, as evidenced by the very strong performance of the 20-year Argentina global bond," said Nick Blakey, debt trader at UBS.
"This cross-over buying was also particularly noticeable in the recent 10-year Mexico deal," he said.

On Wednesday, Argentina priced a $2.0 billion 20-year to yield 462.5 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. The deal was nearly four times oversubscribed, the lead managers said, and was quoted at a 425 b.p. spread on Thursday.
Earlier in the month, Mexico raised $1.0 billion via a 10-year global bond. Launched at 335 b.p. over, the deal has performed well to yield around 295 b.p. over.
"First we saw the high-yield (junk bond) players in the U.S. buying more emerging market corporate paper," said a New York-based syndicate manager.

"What we have seen lately is high-grade investors buying the higher non-investment grade countries, like Argentina and Mexico," he said, adding demand came from bond funds and insurance companies in particular.
Driving the demand for emerging market bonds is a desire for higher yield in a continuing low interest-rate environment.
"(Institutional) investors are keen to buy yield, and following recent spread tightening are extending duration to get the higher returns," said a syndicate manager at a U.S. bank.
"Improved fundamentals in Mexico and Argentina are also boosting their confidence," he said.
Mexico got a lot of good publicity last week when it prepaid money owed the U.S. and the International Monetary Fund. The move further boosted confidence in the region, dealers said.

"For the Mexico deal we saw buying from corporates, from investment trusts who normally only buy investment grade and commercial banks," said Michael Ridley, director of debt syndicate at Salomon Brothers, joint lead of Mexico's global.
"A wide range of investors bought the paper, as well as the usual emerging market credits. There is a search for yield which is quite widespread at the moment," he said.
Over 300 accounts bought the Argentina jumbo bond, with 70 percent of buyers from the U.S., 15 percent from Europe, nine percent from Asia and six percent from Latin America.
U.S. institutional investors are traditionally buyers of longer-dated paper, and this explains why emerging market borrowers have been able to issue such deals recently.
But specialised emerging market investors are also moving out on the curve, dealers said.
"Many investors look at the yield pick-up of a longer-dated bond versus a shorter maturity, and are deciding to go for the higher yield," said a syndicate manager at J.P. Morgan.
Argentina originally planned to issue five- and 20-year tranches, but strong demand for the longer-dated paper led it to scrap the five-year leg.
Historically, Latin America has been more interesting to U.S. investors than Eastern Europe or Asia, but dealers said their focus was broadening.

"U.S. investor interest is changing, particularly in favour of Eastern Europe, an area where there will be a great deal of improvement. Eastern Europe and Russia are a growth market for U.S. investors," said the New York-based syndicate manager.
The big test for the sector would be investor reaction if spreads reverse the current tightening trend, which dealers said could happen if the U.S. Treasury market weakened.
"Buying (from non-emerging market investors) will continue even if spreads don't keep falling," Ridley at Salomon said.
He said these investors had previously not been prepared to consider buying these credits.
"Investors are now a lot more receptive to research and are prepared to do some work to understand the credit," Ridley said.
